steps.why: Rounding keeps the reported value as close as possible to the measured one, so the direction is decided by which side of halfway the dropped digit falls.
common_mistakes: Rounding 3.24 up to 3.3 because the 4 was read as "nearly 5".

recall.must_convey: That a dropped digit below five leaves the previous digit unchanged, and above five raises it by one.
accept: more than five raise by one

steps.memory_tip: Below 5 stays, above 5 rises. Exactly 5 has its own rule.
steps.margin_note: Two lines here, then the 5 rule below.

steps.label: The rule for 5

lines.text: If the dropped digit is exactly 5, round

lines: up and down happen equally often.
steps.why: Always rounding a 5 upward would push a long set of results slightly high. Rounding to the even digit removes that bias. The round-to-even rule applies only when the 5 is the last digit or is followed by zeros. If non-zero digits follow the 5, the value is above halfway, so round up: 3.2501 → 3.3.
common_mistakes: Always rounding a 5 up, which biases a series of measurements upward.

recall.must_convey: That when the dropped digit is exactly five, the preceding digit is rounded to the nearest even number.

steps.memory_tip: 3.25 → 3.2 but 3.35 → 3.4. Land on the even digit both times.
steps.margin_note: Give both examples — one down, one up.

insider_note: Two rules, then one worked pair. The examiner is checking the 5 rule, so give an example of it.
